history.heading: Kaabu and the Portuguese
paragraphs: The region of Guinea-Bissau was part of the Mali Empire, and later the Kaabu kingdom, a Mandinka state, dominated the area until the 19th century. Portuguese navigators arrived in the 1440s, and the coast became a centre of the slave trade, with Cacheu and Bissau as trading posts.
Portugal only established full control over the interior in the early 20th century, after long resistance.

history.heading: Liberation war and independence
paragraphs: Amílcar Cabral founded the PAIGC to fight for the independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, and launched an armed struggle in 1963 that became one of Africa's most successful liberation wars. Cabral was assassinated in January 1973, months before the PAIGC declared independence on 24 September 1973; Portugal recognised it in 1974 after its own revolution.

Since independence, the country has experienced repeated coups and attempted coups, a civil war in 1998–99, and political assassinations. Drug traffickers have used the country as a transit point for cocaine to Europe. In November 2025 the military seized power during the counting of election results.

culture.heading: Peoples and traditions
paragraphs: The main ethnic groups include the Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Manjaco and Papel. Portuguese is official, but Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriol) is the common language. Muslims, Christians and followers of traditional religions all form large communities.
The Bijagós Archipelago, with its matriarchal traditions and rich wildlife, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Gumbe music and Carnival in Bissau are popular.

politics.heading: Political instability
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau is formally a semi-presidential republic, but politics has been marked by frequent conflicts between presidents, prime ministers and parliament, and by military interventions. A military junta took over in November 2025 and announced a transition period.

economy.heading: Cashew economy
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau is one of the world's poorest countries. Cashew nuts account for the vast majority of exports, and most people depend on farming them and on subsistence agriculture and fishing. Fishing licences are an important source of government revenue.
The currency is the West African CFA franc. Instability and weak institutions have hindered development.
